issues.legal_issue: Compensation for acquired land may be assessed by reference to the value on the date of the acquisition notification, and phased acquisition does not by itself invalidate that basis.
material_facts: The challenge concerned compensation assessed by reference to the value of the land when the acquisition notification was published, rather than when possession was taken.
The acquisition was for a public purpose.
The statutory scheme provided for interest on market value after a period of delay in payment and allowed sanctioned post-notification improvements to be considered in awarding compensation.
The challenge to phased acquisition was treated as, in substance, a challenge to the adequacy of compensation.
issues.conclusion: The challenge to assessing compensation by reference to the notification date was rejected; the phased-acquisition objection did not invalidate the acquisition.
issues.legal_principle: Article 31(5) precluded the asserted challenge to the compensation basis for an acquisition for public purpose. Sections 4(3) of the Land Acquisition Amendment and Validation Act, 1957 and 24 of the Land Acquisition Act provided for interest in the specified circumstances and consideration of sanctioned improvements. Section 23 concerned compensation, not procedure. The Court relied on Aflatoon v. Lt. Governor of Delhi, which had upheld the notification and the compensation basis; the validation of phased acquisition under the 1957 Act had been upheld in Udai Ram Sharma v. Union of India, following the issue considered in State of Madhya Pradesh v. Vishnu Prasad Sharma.

predicates.land_acquisition_challenge: A party challenges the basis on which compensation is assessed in a land acquisition proceeding.
predicates.acquisition_for_public_purpose: The land is acquired to serve a public purpose.
predicates.compensation_based_on_notification_date: The compensation assessment uses the land's value when the acquisition notification is published.

issues.definition: When a party challenges compensation in a public-purpose land acquisition and the assessment uses the notification-date value, the challenge to that basis is rejected.

issues.legal_issue: A challenge based on procedural unreasonableness does not succeed when the challenged compensation provision determines compensation rather than prescribing procedure.
material_facts: The challengers argued that the compensation basis was an unreasonable restriction on property rights and invoked procedural reasonableness.
The challenged provision concerned the measure of compensation and did not prescribe the procedure for determining it.
The Court noted that a procedure allowing compensation to be determined without hearing the owner could present a procedural problem, but that was not what the challenged provision did.
issues.conclusion: The compensation provision was not vulnerable to the procedural-unreasonableness challenge advanced.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 19, the Court treated the relevant inquiry as one of procedural reasonableness, drawing on the Bank Nationalisation case. Article 31(5) precluded the challenge to the acquisition and compensation basis in this case. Section 23 of the Land Acquisition Act dealt with compensation and not procedure; a tribunal empowered to determine compensation without hearing the owner could raise a different issue.

predicates.land_acquisition_challenge: A party challenges a rule applied in a land acquisition proceeding.
predicates.challenge_targets_compensation_measure: The challenge concerns how compensation is measured rather than how the decision-making process is conducted.
predicates.provision_does_not_set_procedure: The provision being challenged does not prescribe the procedure for determining compensation.

issues.definition: When a challenge in a land acquisition proceeding targets the compensation measure and the relevant provision does not set procedure, the procedural-unreasonableness challenge is rejected.

issues.legal_issue: A general planned-development purpose is sufficiently specific for an acquisition covering a large area made up of plots owned by different people.
material_facts: The acquisition covered a large area comprising plots belonging to different people.
Planning addressed overcrowding, slums, insanitation, traffic hazards, substandard construction and inadequate civic amenities.
The plan was intended to provide for residential, industrial and commercial needs and to support orderly development.
The acquisition notification stated the purpose as planned development.
issues.conclusion: The stated planned-development purpose was sufficiently particular and was not invalid for vagueness.
issues.legal_principle: Aflatoon v. Lt. Governor of Delhi held that planned development was a public purpose and that, for a large acquisition comprising multiple plots and owners, the purpose could be specified by reference to the acquisition as a whole; it need not identify each particular use of every plot. The Court applied that holding to the public-purpose requirement under sections 4 and 6 of the Land Acquisition Act.

rule.if: land_acquisition_challenge and large_multi_owner_area and acquisition_for_comprehensive_planning and purpose_described_for_whole_area

predicates.land_acquisition_challenge: A party challenges the stated purpose for a land acquisition proceeding.
predicates.large_multi_owner_area: The acquisition covers a large area divided among multiple owners.
predicates.acquisition_for_comprehensive_planning: The land is acquired to address broad planning needs and support orderly development.
predicates.purpose_described_for_whole_area: The notification states a general purpose for the acquisition as a whole rather than specifying each plot's particular use.

issues.definition: When a challenge concerns a large multi-owner acquisition for comprehensive planning and the purpose is stated for the area as a whole, the stated public purpose is sufficiently specific.
